newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Israel police check on Argentine bomb probe.
newsitem.headline: Israel police check on Argentine bomb probe.

text.p: Israeli police head Asaf Hefetz, in Argentina to monitor investigations into the bombing of two Jewish targets, said late on Thursday he hoped Argentine police would solve the crimes in which 115 people were killed.
"I expect a police organisation to do everything it can to solve and jail the guilty," Hefetz told Reuters after a news conference late on Thursday.

In March 1992 an explosion razed the Israeli Embassy in Buenos Aires, killing 29. And in July 1994 a car-bomb at the AMIA Jewish community centre killed 86 and injured hundreds. Both cases are unsolved and the investigations appear to have stalled.

Hefetz, who arrived with three other Israeli police officers, said he had met Interior Minister Carlos Corach and Federal Police Chief Adrian Pelacchi. The Israeli delegation arrived in Buenos Aires at a time when Argentine police were being implicated in corruption and drug-trafficking cases and suspected of being involved in the recent murder of a journalist.

Five officers and non-commissioned officers of the Buenos Aires provincial police were indicted for alleged links to groups that sold the van used to blow up the AMIA. Their indictment caused an institutional crisis that led to the firing of the province's top police authorities.

"I want to think there is a serious, professional organisation which is doing what it needs to do. If that is not the case there is no basis for cooperation," Hefetz said. "My general feeling is the investigation can go on."

He denied his visit was pressure by Israel on the government of Argentine President Carlos Menem. "That's not the case, nor did I receive orders from (Prime Minister Benjamin) Netanyahu. The visit was planned five months ago," he said.

He said Israeli security forces were also concerned about the situation in Ciudad del Este, a Paraguayan town on the border with Brazil and Argentina. Intelligence experts say the town, which has a growing population of immigrants from Middle Eastern countries, may be a hideout for Islamic fundamentalists like those presumed to have bombed the AMIA.
